speakers: Rob Carver (systematic futures trader, author of Systematic Trading, ex-AHL)
summary:
Systematic Investor weekly (Nov 2025) with Rob Carver answering listener questions on backtest robustness, rebalancing, intraday vs end-of-day execution, position sizing and skew, sentiment indicators, ATR; then CalPERS' adoption of the total portfolio approach.
Carver: trend following is a risk premium, backtests must avoid multiple-testing and use rolling selection, dynamic vol targeting beats fixed sizing, trade slow. TPA is promising but vague; could benefit trend following.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: my my personal belief is if anyone can do it then you haven't got an edge
claims.claim: Trend following is a risk premium rather than an edge: anyone with capital and a simple system can do it, so profits compensate for risks others find uncomfortable.
claims.direction: long trend following as risk premium

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: So, we can talk about psychological biases but we can talk about you know, delayed reactions to information.
claims.claim: The two main explanations for why trend following earns money are psychological biases and delayed reactions to information.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the Renaissance Institutional Equity Fund was down 14% in October um and down 8.3% so far this this year
claims.claim: Renaissance public funds (Institutional Equity -14% in Oct 2025, Diversified Alpha -15%) show that even elite quant funds suffer outlier months, making CTAs' 2025 look less bad.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there's always been a big disparity between um the Medallion Fund, which has been closed forever, you know.
claims.claim: Renaissance's closed Medallion fund returns differ massively from its outside funds, possibly because alpha has limited capacity or good ideas are kept inside, and its outside CTA-type fund underperformed.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: A newer category of managed futures exchange-traded funds has outperformed better uh has performed better, sorry, than many established CTA funds.
claims.claim: Cheaper, more transparent managed futures ETFs outperformed many established CTA funds in 2025 and attracted inflows.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they obviously added it in 2023 after the exceptional year in 2022
claims.claim: A Midwestern pension that allocated to CTAs in 2023 after the great 2022 became frustrated: chasing past performance with too short a horizon leads to disappointment.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: market universe this year is really having a huge impact on on returns
claims.claim: In 2025, differences between CTAs, ETFs and replicators were driven by exposure (how much equity, fixed income) and market universe, more than model type, so conclusions about which approach is better are dangerous.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: It's still you know okay to be long in in precious precious metals
claims.claim: In November 2025 trend profits were in precious metals, softs, some oil products and small currencies (NZD, MXN) while equities were the challenge.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: my my risk sizing is probably in line with your trend barometer
claims.claim: Carver's dynamic risk sizing was below average, consistent with a neutral trend barometer (48); he was in a drawdown of just over 10% with biggest short in Bitcoin and net long equities.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: that's not really enough data points for a statistically significant model
claims.claim: Only about four Bitcoin halvings exist, too few observations for a statistically meaningful halving-cycle model.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: CTA Societe Generale CTA index down 69 basis points for the month, down 2.2% for the year.
claims.claim: As of late Nov 2025 SG CTA index -2.2% YTD, SG Trend -1.18%, short-term traders -5.16%, vs MSCI World +16.86% and S&P 500 +14.2%.
claims.indicator: SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-Term Traders indices

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if your holding period is more analogous to mine, which is about, say, an average of a month, um then you don't need to go near tick data.
claims.claim: Backtest data frequency should match holding period: fast strategies need tick data, monthly-holding trend systems need none.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: even delaying your trades by a day, which is what I test in my backtester, shouldn't change your results that much.
claims.claim: A slow strategy should be insensitive to a one-day execution delay; if it is not, there is a problem. This also removes the need to trade at the close.
claims.conditions: for holding periods of about a month

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: 3 to 5 years probably for me is an insufficient amount of time um to to do sort of the calibration testing of strategies.
claims.claim: With monthly holding periods, 3-5 years of build data is too short for calibration and yields non-robust results.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: they also tell you how well you would have performed in the past
claims.claim: A backtest has two aims, finding future strategies and estimating past performance; selecting the best in-sample strategies destroys the second because performance is selected on the same data.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you start with say a thousand strategies and you basically do a rolling process where you you subselect from those strategies depending on the performance you've only seen in the past.
claims.claim: Gold-standard backtest: start with many strategies, roll forward and reweight using only past performance, which gives an honest historic result and a final strategy mix.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you've got no information, so you just include all the strategies backtest including ones that are beep as well as ones that are good.
claims.claim: In a rolling selection backtest, begin with all strategies equal weighted (flat performance if half are bad) and shift weight to good ones as evidence accrues.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: just by luck 10 of them are going to be amazing
claims.claim: Multiple testing: picking the top 1% of a thousand strategies selects luck, since flat strategies will produce 10 amazing ones by chance; choosing too few on insufficient data is the main flaw.
claims.conditions: unless trading very short time frames

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Yes, your 10 superstars would would have a higher weight than the others, but they by no means would they be filling the entire portfolio up.
claims.claim: With statistically robust weighting, the best strategies get higher weights but others stay, since a few years of data cannot prove 10 strategies are best.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Trading costs should be in there from the very start.
claims.claim: Include trading costs in the backtest from the beginning; strategies that do not make money before slippage should not be considered.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: then I think it's probably appropriate to do this re-optimization of weights to strategies about every year, say.
claims.claim: With monthly holding, reoptimise strategy weights about annually (AHL used an annual refit); more frequent adds nothing.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I've refitted my my weights on average about every 3 years.
claims.claim: With 55 years of data an extra year adds under 2%, so Carver refits weights about every three years, typically only when other changes are made.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: You're going to be somewhere between those two.
claims.claim: Trading during the day after the previous close gives performance between trading at the previous close and at the next close, so if backtests at both are close results are robust.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: You want to spread your trades throughout the day and try and reduce your market impact as much as possible.
claims.claim: Institutional-size slow trend systems should spread execution through the day to cut impact, and can run dynamic optimisation continuously to smooth trades, though reacting to big intraday moves can lose if prices bounce back.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's harder to to do your trades with sort of passive limit orders
claims.claim: Intraday trend trading has higher costs because more trades are needed and passive limit orders do not work when catching a short trend.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: they tend to start to decline for holding periods shorter than about a month or a couple of weeks, depending on the asset class.
claims.claim: Trend efficacy declines for holding periods below roughly a month or two weeks, and below about one hour mean reversion appears.
claims.conditions: shorter than 1 month; sub-hour is mean reversion

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: It's really the diversification and and the longer holding period and all that stuff that makes it a little bit difficult, makes it a little bit uncomfortable, that makes it work.
claims.claim: Trend following is designed to work across many asset classes with long holding periods, not on single asset classes or at fast speeds; the discomfort is what earns the premium.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: are spending too much in costs, but you know, taking too much leverage, and over fitting the trading systems.
claims.claim: Three things kill systematic traders: excessive costs, excessive leverage and overfitting.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you can design your systems to react differently from entries to exits.
claims.claim: Trend systems can differentiate speeds between entry and exit signals, and risk management and use of volatility have evolved, without changing the core rules.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: things that have positive skew um may not have as good a sharp ratio, but may produce you a better geometric return.
claims.claim: Choosing between static and dynamic sizing depends on objective: positive skew improves geometric return but hurts Sharpe, negative skew the opposite.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you you constantly evaluate your positions according to things like volatility, strength of your trends
claims.claim: Continuous trading re-evaluates positions on volatility, trend strength and possibly account size, and fixed-vol-target systems are also affected by correlations.
claims.direction: reduce size as vol or losses rise

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you're not changing your position according to volatility, that leap in price which of course also increases volatility, you'd keep your you'd keep your position the same size
claims.claim: Without volatility scaling a sudden jump (cocoa) is held at full size, giving outsized positive outlier returns and positive skew but lower Sharpe.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's not worth doing fixed vol position sizing because the the additional skew you get does not pay you for the loss in sharp, which is substantial.
claims.claim: Theory shows that the skew gained from not scaling position size to volatility does not compensate for the Sharpe lost, giving lower CAGR than dynamic vol sizing.
claims.conditions: theory rather than empirical; assumes leverage can be adjusted

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if I apply just a little bit of extra leverage to my system, I could very easily beat their geometric returns
claims.claim: A high-Sharpe, less skewed system with a bit more leverage can beat the geometric return of high-skew, high-vol CTAs.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you're trying to trade off two things. The benefits you'd get from having your position close to what your optimal position should be and the cost of trading to get there.
claims.claim: Rebalancing frequency trades off tracking the optimal position against trading costs.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: If I was to to rebalance, say, every day without fail, then some days I'll be buying, some days I'll be selling.
claims.claim: Daily rebalancing to a noisy volatility estimate creates churn and extra trading costs that exceed the benefit.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there is an a solution to this conundrum, and that's to use um either buffering or smoothing.
claims.claim: Buffering (trade only if far from optimum) or smoothing (moving average of target position, EWMA vol) allows frequent rebalancing without extra cost.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I'd say you should treat both kinds of volatility the same.
claims.claim: Volatility should be treated symmetrically for sizing: upside risk equals downside risk and a coin flip away from big gains turning into big losses.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: something with that's got very heavy negative skew would tend to be underpriced because people don't like it
claims.claim: Carver's skew signal buys assets with heavy negative historic skew, which is underpriced because investors dislike it; a skew signal is a sentiment proxy.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: essentially it's massively in-sample fitted and therefore of course it looks very good.
claims.claim: Third-party sentiment indicators or models offered by sell-side are typically in-sample fitted, so be wary and build in-house.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: sort of various options ratios as well you can use.
claims.claim: Skew, option ratios and VIX level are valid sentiment proxies for predicting prices though Carver does not use them.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: So, in this that that simple example where you've got very strong negative auto correlation, the daily standard deviation is much higher than the annual standard deviation.
claims.claim: Volatility scaling by sqrt(time) holds only with zero autocorrelation; negative autocorrelation makes daily vol exceed annualised vol, positive the opposite.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there should be a sort of multiple of around square root of five between those two values in theory.
claims.claim: Weekly ATR should be about sqrt(5) times daily ATR under zero autocorrelation.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I would use daily daily daily price changes to calculate my ATRs
claims.claim: More frequent data gives more accurate volatility estimates, though backtests can run weekly for weekly systems.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: only only execute those that have moved in your favor.
claims.claim: Cheap execution idea: slow momentum signals executed the next day only if price has moved in your favour (buy only after dip) combines slow trend with short-term mean reversion.
claims.indicator: previous close vs next day price
claims.direction: buy after dips, sell after rallies for slow signals
claims.conditions: needs test that delay beyond one day does not hurt

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they voted in favor of adopting the total portfolio approach TPA which is going to replace their existing strategic asset allocation the SAA model.
claims.claim: CalPERS board adopted the total portfolio approach (from July 2026) replacing SAA, with a reference portfolio of 75% equities/25% bonds.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: whether this is just going to be an easy an excuse to jam more private equity.
claims.claim: Carver cynically suggests TPA may be an excuse to add more private assets rather than diversifiers.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's a very kind of structured top-down process, basically.
claims.claim: SAA is top-down: set return, risk and correlation expectations, build the efficient frontier, choose the max Sharpe or minimum risk meeting hurdle, then fill sleeves (hedge funds, private credit, CTAs) as boxes.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I happen to put into one of my boxes something that's highly correlated to something in another box, that does not enter into the decision process.
claims.claim: SAA box structure ignores correlations across boxes, e.g. a CTA correlated to Danish equities added to a Danish-equity-heavy portfolio.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: we look at the thing as a whole
claims.claim: TPA evaluates additions holistically (add CTA, dial down equities, or replace), which should favour diversifying strategies.
claims.direction: more allocation to diversifiers if adopted

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: a quant would say something like maximize uh utility function where you input the correlation the standard deviation and the expected vector of mean returns plus your constraints
claims.claim: TPA lacks formal definition; a quant formulation would be Markowitz optimisation with utility and constraints.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: unlike proper tail protection funds, we can't guarantee that we'll make you money in in a in a down market.
claims.claim: CTAs do not fit in the hedge fund box or the tail-protection box because their correlation is different, they have no crisis guarantee but a positive Sharpe, so portfolio-level assessment helps them.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if they start doing it, then then I think that will really will be a game-changer
claims.claim: If large quant-heavy allocators like ADIA adopt TPA with formal publications, it could be a game-changer for trend following allocations.
